animals.behavior_notes: California Red-legged Frogs, the largest native frog in the western US, are most active during their winter and early spring breeding season when they call from dense vegetation in ponds and slow streams. As a federally threatened species, their populations are fragmented and significantly reduced from historical levels.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit freshwater ponds and slow-moving streams at Point Reyes at dusk after winter rains — listen for the stuttering, low-pitched grunting call. Stay on trails and avoid disturbing aquatic vegetation where egg masses may be attached.

animals.name: Wood Frog
animals.behavior_notes: Wood Frogs are famous for being among the first amphibians to emerge each spring, often breeding in temporary vernal pools while snow is still on the ground nearby. Their explosive breeding aggregations last only a few days, with hundreds of frogs congregating and calling with a distinctive duck-like quacking chorus.
animals.viewing_tips: Listen for the rapid, clucking quack of Wood Frog choruses near vernal pools and woodland ponds on the first warm, rainy nights of late winter or very early spring. The breeding window is extremely brief — often just 3–5 days — so be ready to visit as soon as temperatures reach the mid-40s°F.

animals.name: American Toad
animals.behavior_notes: American Toads emerge in spring to breed in shallow ponds, marshes, and slow streams, with males producing a long, melodious trill that can last 20–30 seconds. After breeding, they disperse widely into forests, gardens, and meadows where they are commonly encountered on warm summer evenings hunting insects.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit garden edges, forest paths, and pond margins at dusk — American Toads are one of the most commonly encountered amphibians in the eastern US and are rarely shy. During breeding season, ponds can contain dozens of calling males, making for an extraordinary auditory experience.

animals.name: Spotted Salamander
animals.behavior_notes: Spotted Salamanders undertake dramatic mass migrations on the first warm, rainy nights of late winter, emerging from underground burrows and traveling to ancestral vernal pools to breed — often the very same pools where they hatched. Their bold yellow spots on jet-black bodies make them one of the most visually striking salamanders in North America.
animals.viewing_tips: On the first rainy night when temperatures exceed 40°F in late February or March, drive slowly near woodland vernal pools and check roadsides with a flashlight — migrating adults can number in the hundreds at a single pool. Arrive after dark for the best chance of witnessing this spectacular annual event.

animals.name: Axolotl
parks: Xochimilco Ecological Park (not a US NP — see viewing_tips)
animals.behavior_notes: Axolotls are critically endangered and native to Lake Xochimilco in Mexico City, Mexico. They are not found in the wild in the United States and exist in the US only in captivity, research institutions, and aquariums.
animals.viewing_tips: There are no wild axolotl populations in the US. For viewing, visit accredited aquariums such as the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, IL or the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco, CA. Wild observation is not possible within US borders.

animals.name: Spring Peeper
animals.behavior_notes: Spring Peepers emerge from winter dormancy as early as late February and begin calling loudly at dusk from wetland edges, vernal pools, and pond margins. Males congregate in dense choruses to attract females, producing the iconic high-pitched peeping sound synonymous with the arrival of spring.
animals.viewing_tips: Listen for large choruses near shallow wetlands, swamps, and forest ponds after dark on warm, rainy evenings when temperatures exceed 40°F. Spotting them visually is difficult due to their small size (under 1.5 inches) and camouflaged coloring — use a flashlight and look for the inflated vocal sac on calling males near the water's edge.

animals.name: Atlantic Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Atlantic salmon return to natal rivers in fall to spawn, making their upstream runs most visible in October and November. They can be observed leaping over obstacles in rivers draining into the Gulf of Maine.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit the Narraguagus or Machias rivers near Acadia in October; look for fish jumping at natural falls or riffles at dawn. Wild Atlantic salmon are critically rare in the US — sightings are not guaranteed.

animals.name: Chinook Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Chinook salmon undertake massive fall spawning runs up coastal rivers, with large individuals visible in clear shallow riffles. Their size — often exceeding 30 pounds — makes them easier to spot than smaller salmon species.
animals.viewing_tips: The Hoh and Queets rivers in Olympic National Park offer excellent fall viewing; wade to riverbanks and look for large dark shapes holding in current or actively spawning on gravel beds.

animals.name: Sockeye Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Sockeye turn vivid red during their summer spawning runs, making them among the most visually striking salmon. At Brooks Falls in Katmai, massive concentrations gather below the falls waiting to leap upstream.
animals.viewing_tips: Brooks Falls viewing platforms at Katmai offer world-class sockeye and brown bear viewing simultaneously in July; arrive early in the season for peak fish concentrations and bear activity.

animals.name: Coho Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Coho salmon enter freshwater rivers in fall, peaking later than Chinook, and are often seen in smaller tributaries and side channels. They are aggressive and acrobatic, frequently jumping in lower river sections.
animals.viewing_tips: Check smaller coastal streams and river mouths in Olympic National Park's Quinault and Sol Duc drainages in November; polarized sunglasses help spot fish holding in pools below riffles.

animals.name: Steelhead Trout
animals.behavior_notes: Steelhead are sea-run rainbow trout that return to rivers in winter and early spring to spawn, favoring high, cold water flows after rain events. They hold in deep pools and runs, often visible in clear water on sunny days.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit the Smith or Klamath rivers adjacent to Redwood National Park after winter rains raise river levels; look into deep green pools from bridge vantages for large silver fish finning in current.

animals.name: Lake Sturgeon
animals.behavior_notes: Lake sturgeon spawn in spring on rocky river shoals, congregating in large numbers in the St. Mary's River and Lake Superior tributaries. Adults may roll and thrash at the surface during spawning activity.
animals.viewing_tips: The Sturgeon River near Baraga, MI and the St. Mary's River at Sault Ste. Marie see reliable May spawning runs; observe from bridges or riverbanks at first light without disturbing fish on redds.

animals.name: White Sturgeon
parks: Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area
animals.behavior_notes: White sturgeon, the largest freshwater fish in North America, congregate in the Columbia River in spring for spawning, sometimes breaching dramatically near the surface. They prefer deep, slow pools near dam tailwaters.
animals.viewing_tips: Bonneville Dam on the Columbia River has underwater viewing windows where sturgeon are frequently visible year-round; boat-based viewing tours below the dam in April–May offer the best surface sightings.

animals.name: Paddlefish
animals.behavior_notes: Paddlefish migrate upstream in early spring to spawn on gravel bars when water temperatures reach 50–60°F, occasionally rolling at the surface or visible in clear shallows. They filter-feed on zooplankton and are rarely seen leaping.
animals.viewing_tips: The Osage and Niangua rivers in Missouri and the Yellowstone River in Montana offer spring paddlefish sightings; look for their distinctive paddle-shaped rostrum breaking the surface in slow, clear stretches at dawn.

animals.name: Alligator Gar
animals.behavior_notes: Alligator gar are most active in summer in slow backwaters, oxbow lakes, and bayous of the Gulf Coast. They frequently surface to gulp air and can be spotted rolling or basking near the surface in calm water.
animals.viewing_tips: Paddle quiet backwater sloughs in Big Thicket or Trinity River National Wildlife Refuge at first light; look for large dark torpedo shapes near the surface or listen for the splash of their air-gulping behavior.

animals.name: Manta Ray
animals.behavior_notes: Oceanic manta rays visit warm nearshore waters and reef systems in summer to feed on plankton blooms, often leaping dramatically from the water or performing slow barrel rolls near the surface while feeding.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel or dive the outer reefs of Biscayne National Park in summer or join a guided dive tour in the Florida Keys; mantas are more reliably encountered in Hawaii around Kona's night dive sites near artificial lights that attract plankton.

animals.name: Whale Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Whale sharks congregate near warm surface waters in summer months, often feeding on fish spawn and plankton blooms. They are slow, filter-feeding giants that tend to linger near the surface, making sightings possible from boats.
animals.viewing_tips: Book a dive or snorkel charter out of Key West or Marathon in summer; sightings are opportunistic so scan the surface from the bow for their distinctive spotted pattern and broad flat head.

animals.name: Hammerhead Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Great hammerheads and scalloped hammerheads patrol shallow reef edges and sandy flats during summer, hunting stingrays and fish. They are more active at dawn and dusk when prey is abundant near the reef structure.
animals.viewing_tips: Join a guided dive trip out of Homestead Bayfront Park into Biscayne's reef zones; hammerheads are shy so stay calm, avoid sudden movements, and keep a respectful distance if encountered.

animals.name: Great White Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Great white sharks aggregate around the Northern Channel Islands in fall and winter to prey on pinnipeds such as elephant seals and sea lions. They are most active in morning hours near seal haul-out areas.
animals.viewing_tips: Book a live-aboard dive or wildlife boat tour departing from Ventura or Oxnard; scan the surface near seal colonies at Anacapa and San Miguel islands for dorsal fins or surface breach activity.

animals.name: Bull Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Bull sharks are uniquely adapted to tolerate freshwater and regularly enter the estuaries, rivers, and mangrove creeks of the Everglades in warm months. They are opportunistic hunters most active around tidal changes at dawn and dusk.
animals.viewing_tips: Take an airboat or kayak tour through the Ten Thousand Islands or Flamingo area estuaries; watch for shark movement in tannin-colored shallow water near mangrove edges, especially during incoming tides.

animals.name: Coelacanth
animals.behavior_notes: Coelacanths are deep-sea fish found in the Indian Ocean and Indonesian waters, not present in US waters. They inhabit submarine cave systems at depths of 100–400 meters and are rarely encountered even in their native range.
animals.viewing_tips: Coelacanths do not occur in the wild within the United States; wild viewing is not possible for US residents without traveling to Tanzania, South Africa, or Indonesia. Visit a natural history museum such as the Smithsonian to see preserved specimens.

animals.name: Brook Trout
animals.behavior_notes: Brook trout are native to the cold, clear headwater streams of the Appalachians and are most active in spring and fall when water temperatures are ideal. They feed actively in early morning, rising to the surface for insects and small invertebrates.
animals.viewing_tips: Wade quietly into the headwater streams along Skyline Drive such as the upper Rapidan River or Hazel River; polarized sunglasses will help you spot colorful brookies holding in pools below riffles in clear shallow runs.

animals.name: Largemouth Bass
animals.behavior_notes: Largemouth bass are most active in spring during spawning season when water temperatures reach 60–75°F, and again in fall as they feed aggressively before winter. They cruise shallow vegetated areas and structure edges at dawn and dusk.
animals.viewing_tips: Canoe or kayak the Current or Jacks Fork rivers at first light; peer into clear pools near submerged logs and aquatic vegetation where bass hold in ambush positions, and they are often visible in the gin-clear Ozark spring-fed water.

animals.name: Monarch Butterfly
animals.behavior_notes: Monarchs aggregate in large roosts during fall migration, often clustering on trees overnight. On warm sunny mornings they take flight and feed on nectar-rich wildflowers to fuel their journey south.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit coastal stopover sites in September and October and look for clusters on goldenrod, milkweed, and trees. Calm, sunny mornings after a cool night produce the most dramatic sightings.

animals.name: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail
animals.behavior_notes: Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are active nectarers visiting garden flowers, thistles, and wild bergamot throughout the warm months. Males frequently puddle on moist soil and gravel roads to extract minerals.
animals.viewing_tips: Look along woodland edges and forest roads where wildflowers are blooming. Males are easy to spot puddling on damp gravel paths in the morning hours.

animals.name: Painted Lady Butterfly
animals.behavior_notes: Painted Ladies are strong migratory fliers and can appear in massive irruption years when thistle host plants are abundant. They actively nectar on thistles, asters, and composites throughout the warmest parts of the day.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan open meadows and roadsides for thistles during midday sunshine. Migration years following wet winters in the Southwest can produce extraordinary numbers.

animals.name: Luna Moth
animals.behavior_notes: Luna Moths are nocturnal and adults do not feed, living only about a week as adults solely to mate. They are most active on warm, humid nights and are attracted to lights near wooded areas with walnut, sweetgum, or birch trees.
animals.viewing_tips: Check porch lights and lit windows near deciduous forest on warm, calm, humid nights in spring. Look carefully on tree trunks and walls near light sources just after dark.

animals.name: Cecropia Moth
animals.behavior_notes: Cecropia Moths are North America's largest native moth and are strictly nocturnal, flying on warm nights to locate mates by pheromone detection. Adults do not eat and live only 1–2 weeks, concentrating all energy on reproduction.
animals.viewing_tips: Set up a white sheet with a UV blacklight near woodland edges on warm nights above 55°F with low wind. Females can sometimes be found resting near emergence sites just after dawn.

animals.name: American Bumble Bee
animals.behavior_notes: American Bumble Bees are among the most imperiled native bees in North America and have declined sharply in the Midwest. Workers forage actively on clovers, prairie wildflowers, and sunflowers during warm sunny mornings.
animals.viewing_tips: Focus on native prairie remnants with diverse wildflowers; look on coneflowers, bergamot, and milkweed. This species is now rare — photograph and report sightings to Bumble Bee Watch to aid conservation.

animals.name: Firefly (Eastern)
animals.behavior_notes: Eastern Fireflies begin flashing roughly 30–45 minutes after sunset during warm, humid evenings in June and July. Males fly low over vegetation and produce species-specific flash patterns to attract perched females.
animals.viewing_tips: Find a dark meadow or forest edge away from artificial lights and wait quietly after sunset. Great Smoky Mountains NP hosts famous synchronous firefly events in early June — permits are required for peak viewing.

animals.name: Periodical Cicada
animals.behavior_notes: Periodical Cicadas emerge in massive synchronized broods after 13 or 17 years underground once soil temperatures reach 64°F at 8 inches depth. Males immediately begin loud chorusing to attract females, with sound levels reaching up to 90 decibels.
animals.viewing_tips: Emergence is highly localized by brood — check USGS Cicada Tracker or iNaturalist to identify which brood is active in your region and year. Look on deciduous tree trunks in hardwood forests for emerging nymphs at night.

animals.name: Dragonfly (Common Green Darner)
animals.behavior_notes: Common Green Darners are one of the few migratory dragonflies in North America, forming large southward-moving swarms along the Atlantic Coast in late summer and fall. They are strong, fast fliers that hunt smaller insects on the wing near ponds, marshes, and open fields.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit coastal wetlands and pond edges in late August through October and look for large mixed-species swarms hunting over open water and meadows. Cool mornings after cold fronts concentrate migrating individuals near the coast.

animals.name: Praying Mantis
animals.behavior_notes: Praying Mantises reach adult size by late summer and are most conspicuous in August through October when they are full-grown and actively hunting in tall vegetation. Females grow especially large as they develop eggs and can be found waiting motionlessly among flowers and grasses for prey.
animals.viewing_tips: Search slowly through tall wildflower patches, goldenrod, and garden borders in late summer — their cryptic coloration makes patience essential. Look for them perched and motionless facing down on flower stems in the morning sun.

animals.name: Walking Stick
animals.behavior_notes: Walking sticks are most active at dusk and night during warm summer months when they emerge to feed on leaves. They remain motionless during the day, making nocturnal searches far more productive.
animals.viewing_tips: Bring a UV or red-beam flashlight and scan oak and deciduous shrub foliage slowly at night. Look for elongated shapes along stems and leaf edges that may be swaying gently to mimic a twig in the breeze.

animals.name: Tarantula (Desert Blonde)
animals.behavior_notes: Male desert blonde tarantulas roam widely in late summer and fall in search of females, making them far more visible than at any other time of year. This mating migration often occurs around sunset and into the early evening hours.
animals.viewing_tips: Drive desert roads at low speed near dusk in the Sonoran Desert during September and October — males crossing roads are the most reliable sighting. The Santa Rita and Rincon Mountain areas of Saguaro NP are well-known hotspots.

animals.name: Black Widow Spider
animals.behavior_notes: Black widow spiders become more active in warmer months and are most detectable at dusk when females sit in the center of their irregular webs waiting for prey. They prefer sheltered, dark recesses such as rock crevices, wood piles, and the undersides of ledges.
animals.viewing_tips: Search carefully under rocks, inside hollow logs, and along the base of desert shrubs with a flashlight after dark — the spider's jet-black abdomen with red hourglass marking is distinctive. Never reach into crevices without visual confirmation; maintain safe distance and do not handle.

animals.name: American Horseshoe Crab
animals.behavior_notes: Horseshoe crabs come ashore in massive spawning aggregations during May and June, timed to high tides near full and new moons. Females crawl onto sandy beaches to lay eggs while smaller males cluster around them, making this one of the most dramatic invertebrate spectacles on the Atlantic coast.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit Delaware Bay beaches such as Slaughter Beach or Prime Hook NWR on a high tide night within a few days of the full or new moon in late May for peak numbers. Cape Hatteras and Virginia barrier island beaches also host reliable spawning events.

animals.name: Giant Water Bug
animals.behavior_notes: Giant water bugs become highly active in spring and early summer as water temperatures rise and prey activity increases in freshwater wetlands and slow-moving streams. Adults frequently fly between water bodies at night and are attracted to lights near ponds and marshes.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan the surface and shallow margins of slow-moving freshwater pools and swamp edges with a flashlight at dusk — these large, flattened brown bugs can be 2–3 inches long and are surprisingly visible once your eye adjusts. Lights near water at night will often attract flying individuals.

animals.name: Pacific Octopus
animals.behavior_notes: Pacific octopuses are most active during cooler months when they hunt crabs and fish in rocky intertidal zones. They are solitary and tend to emerge from dens at dawn and dusk to forage.
animals.viewing_tips: Look in rocky tide pools and kelp beds during low tide; bring a flashlight for den openings and watch for color changes in rocks that may actually be a camouflaged octopus.

animals.name: Giant Pacific Octopus
animals.behavior_notes: Giant Pacific octopuses, the world's largest octopus species, are more active in winter as they den in deeper rocky habitats and emerge to hunt. Females guard egg clutches in dens for months during winter breeding season.
animals.viewing_tips: Best observed via scuba diving or snorkeling in protected coves; shore-based viewing is rare but possible at very low tides in rocky subtidal zones of the Pacific Northwest coast.

animals.name: Bioluminescent Dinoflagellates
animals.behavior_notes: Bioluminescent dinoflagellates bloom in warm, nutrient-rich coastal waters during summer months and emit blue-green light when disturbed by wave action or movement. Blooms are most spectacular on moonless nights.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit a calm bay or lagoon on a moonless night and look for glowing blue light in breaking waves or where you stir the water with your hand; Mosquito Bay in Puerto Rico and some California bays are prime spots.

animals.name: Jellyfish (Moon)
animals.behavior_notes: Moon jellyfish aggregate in large numbers along coastlines during summer when water temperatures rise, often washing into shallow bays and coves. They drift passively with currents and tides, making calm days ideal for sightings.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan calm shallow bays and harbors from docks or kayaks during summer; after onshore winds, beaches often have stranded specimens — avoid touching as tentacles can still sting.

animals.name: Dungeness Crab
animals.behavior_notes: Dungeness crabs are most active in winter months, moving into shallower nearshore waters to feed and mate. They are nocturnal foragers and can be spotted in sandy-bottomed tide pools and estuaries at low tide.
animals.viewing_tips: Check rocky tide pools and sandy estuaries during extreme low tides in winter; pier pilings are excellent observation points and crabbing docks often allow close views of caught specimens.

animals.name: American Lobster
animals.behavior_notes: American lobsters move into shallower nearshore rocky habitats during summer as water warms, making them more accessible to shore-based observers. They emerge from rocky dens at dusk to forage for urchins, mussels, and fish.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel or scuba dive along rocky ledges in sheltered coves at dusk for the best chance of seeing active lobsters; tide pool exploration during very low tides occasionally reveals juveniles under rocks.

animals.name: Coral (Elkhorn)
animals.behavior_notes: Elkhorn coral is a critically endangered reef-building species found in shallow Florida reef tracts; summer brings annual spawning events where corals release egg-sperm bundles into the water column. Colonies are best viewed in calm, clear water with good visibility.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkeling or scuba diving in the shallow reef tracts of Dry Tortugas and Biscayne NP offers the best views; water clarity is best in calm summer mornings — note this species is federally threatened so do not touch or anchor near reefs.

animals.name: Coral (Brain)
animals.behavior_notes: Brain corals are slow-growing, dome-shaped corals that spawn during late summer full moons, releasing gametes in synchrony with other reef corals. They are more resilient than branching corals and remain visible year-round on shallow reefs.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel or dive Florida and USVI reefs at midday when visibility peaks; look for the distinctive grooved dome shapes at depths of 3–30 feet along reef margins — calm days with light winds provide the clearest water conditions.

animals.name: Sea Anemone
animals.behavior_notes: Sea anemones are sessile predators that extend their colorful tentacles to capture plankton and small fish during high water; they retract tightly when exposed at low tide, so the best views occur when tide pools are still partially submerged. Spring low tides expose the richest intertidal zones.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit tide pools during a minus tide in spring when the lowest zones are exposed; look in shaded crevices and under ledges for green, pink, and purple anemones — Olympic NP's Rialto Beach and Acadia's Schoodic Peninsula are top sites.

animals.name: Starfish (Sunflower Sea Star)
animals.behavior_notes: The sunflower sea star is a critically endangered species decimated by sea star wasting disease since 2013, with populations reduced by over 90%; surviving individuals are occasionally found in cooler subtidal habitats during fall. Recovery efforts are underway but wild sightings are now extremely rare.
animals.viewing_tips: This species is critically endangered and rarely seen in the wild — if spotted, report the sighting to the Sea Star Wasting Disease monitoring network; subtidal scuba diving in the Pacific Northwest offers the best slim chance of an encounter.

animals.name: Pacific Sea Nettle
animals.behavior_notes: Pacific Sea Nettles drift with ocean currents in late summer, often forming large aggregations near the surface as warmer water temperatures promote blooms. Their long trailing tentacles and reddish-orange bells are most visible when sunlight penetrates calm, clear water.
animals.viewing_tips: Take a boat or kayak tour around Channel Islands or along the Monterey Bay coastline in late summer for the best chance of spotting surface blooms. Calm days with minimal wind offer the clearest water visibility for observing jellies near the surface.

animals.name: Mantis Shrimp
animals.behavior_notes: Mantis shrimp are most active at dawn and dusk, emerging from burrows in sandy or rubble-strewn seafloors to hunt prey during warmer spring months. During this period they are more territorial and frequently spotted near coral rubble and seagrass beds in shallow reef environments.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkeling or shallow-water scuba diving over coral rubble and sandy patches in Biscayne Bay gives the best opportunity to spot mantis shrimp peering from their burrows. Look carefully into small crevices and holes in the reef substrate — they can be well-camouflaged and extremely fast.
